newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori's star dips in Peru after hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori's star dips in Peru after hostage crisis.

text.p: Toasted at home and abroad for masterminding a spectacular end to a four-month hostage siege, President Alberto Fujimori now finds his popularity at its lowest as Peruvians recoil at the authoritarian style his political career was built on.

Fujimori's surge in domestic popularity after the April 22 hostage rescue vanished within days. Now he is hammered daily in opinion polls that put him at the lowest approval level of his seven-year presidency -- below 30 percent -- and show nearly half of Peruvians believe they live in a dictatorship.

Compounding this slide, Fujimori recently has faced the biggest street protests in Lima for years, and is seeing a newly-buoyant opposition crawl out of the hole it was dumped in by two electoral maulings in 1990 and 1995.

On his customary election-style tours of Lima shantytowns and remote Andean or jungle communities, the crowds are noticeably smaller and less enthusiastic. Heckling, previously unheard of, is now common.

"Because of his political mistakes, summarized by an uncontrolled greed for power and an increasing arrogance in the exercise of this, the people are starting to turn their back on him," wrote columnist Manuel D'Ornellas, whose normally pro-government daily Expreso has begun to attack the president.

It is a far cry from Fujimori's triumphant tank-top appearance and street parade on April 22, minutes after his military defeated the Tupac Amaru rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home.
Then his popularity in domestic opinion polls surged to 70 percent and he was deluged with congratulatory telegrams ranging from U.S. President Bill Clinton to Pope John Paul.

Some analysts and critics point to Fujimori's allegedly crude political manipulation of the hostage rescue in its immediate aftermath. His televised walk beside Tupac Amaru leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini's bloodied corpse inside the gutted mansion was deemed particularly unsavory.

The government's refusal to release all the 14 slain rebels' corpses to their families, plus its reluctance to investigate claims some were executed, also took some of the shine off the military victory.

But most observers agree it was the government's political manoeuvres after the crisis that brought Fujimori's undignified tumble in the polls. Government-controlled Congress' dismissal in May of three constitutional court judges blocking a possible third election bid by Fujimori in 2000 has particularly incensed the public.

The torture of an intelligence agent by colleagues -- for allegedly leaking to the media government plans to silence the opposition -- highlighted excesses by the powerful security forces. And crude moves against the media have further irked the public.
"When you ask those who disapprove of Fujimori why, most reply because he is a dictator," said Bernardo Verjovsky, head of local pollster Analistas y Consultores.

By contrast, Lima's increasingly popular independent mayor Alberto Andrade is soaring in the polls, with twice as many Peruvians saying they would vote for him in a general election than for Fujimori.

The growing opposition to Fujimori's firm hand -- which was widely applauded when turned on leftist guerrillas and a chaotic economy in the early 1990s -- has compounded deep public frustration at Peru's unrelieved social problems.

Fujimori's remarkable macroeconomic reforms, which tamed runaway inflation and turned economic contraction into steady growth, and his virtual defeat of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) and Shining Path guerrillas are fading in the memory. Now Peruvians are more likely to identify their leader with low wages, high unemployment and deep-rooted poverty.

"Fujimori has been used up politically. He has been in office for too long and the bloom has fallen off the rose," said U.S. academic and Peru specialist David Scott Palmer in a telephone interview from Boston. "After the successful end to the hostage crisis, Fujimori became a little hot-headed."

Some fear Fujimori may seek a dramatic solution like a new border conflict with neighbouring Ecuador to distract public attention and unite the nation behind him. But most of his backers hope the government's new anti-poverty policies, at a cost of $2.7 billion between now and 2000, will do the trick.

"I am confident that this situation will be resolved in the short term, when the public perceives the concrete results of the fight against poverty," said Genaro Colchado, political secretary of Fujimori's Change 90-New Majority movement.
